scenario: AITA for refusing to have biological children with my wife? | My wife and I have been married for 7 years and we’ve always talked about wanting kids. We’re both 29 years old and started trying to conceive about a year ago but have been unsuccessful. We recently decided to get checked out by a fertility specialist and opted to have extensive genetic testing done. The genetic counselor said there isn’t a reason they can point to as for why we haven’t conceived yet, but the bad news is that we are both carriers of a genetic disease that could cause our children to go blind. The risk of having a blind child is about 25% with each pregnancy. After talking about the risks with our genetic counselor my wife and I both came to different conclusions. She still wants to experience pregnancy and childbirth and is okay with taking the 25% chance. I’m not. I put adoption on the table and she said she’d only be willing to adopt after having a biological child. She says donor sperm isn’t an option because she wants to have *my* kids and that I’m taking that option away from her over a “small” risk. Two night ago we had really bad fight over it. Hurtful things were said by both of us. During the fight I said that pregnancy is hard and most people suffer through it so It’s not like she’s experiencing a great loss. She can keep her flat stomach and not have to suffer through 9 months of sickness. I told her that her mindset is negative. She disagreed with that and said she see’s nothing to be positive about. She called me a coward for wanting to let my kids be fathered by a donor. I responded that of course she’s never going to see the positive in the situation because she’s 100% negative, just like all of her pregnancy tests were the last year and how they always will be. That’s the line that caused her to start sobbing and leave the house. She packed a bag and told me she was going to stay with her sister and that she’d call me when she was ready to talk. She’s been gone for two nights now. It will be three if she doesn’t come back tonight. I don’t want to extend the olive branch and call her first because I’m still pissed. I don’t know if this post is even a question or a cry for help at this point. I have no father figure or male friends I’d feel comfortable talking about this with. Instead I’m asking strangers on reddit because I’m drunk and at rock bottom. Tonight will be the third night alone in my house drinking by myself and going to bed alone and that terrifies me. Things were completely different a week ago. This sucks. After typing all this out, even I think I’m an asshole.

Here’s why: ### **1. You’re Not an Asshole (But You’re Human)** Your wife’s reaction—especially her sobbing and leaving—is a sign of deep hurt, not just disagreement. Calling her "negative" or comparing her pregnancy tests to her mindset was cruel, even if you were frustrated. You’re both grieving the loss of the "easy" path to parenthood, and your wife is processing that differently. Her insistence on biological children isn’t irrational; it’s tied to identity, connection, and her own hopes for motherhood. **Her pain isn’t "negative"—it’s real.** ### **2. This Isn’t About "Cowardice" or "Suffering"** - **Pregnancy isn’t a noble sacrifice.** It’s a biological process with physical, emotional, and psychological tolls—some women thrive through it, others struggle. Dismissing her desire for it as "not a great loss" minimizes her feelings. - **Adoption isn’t a "backup plan."** It’s a meaningful, loving way to build a family, but it’s not the same as biological parenthood. Her insistence on *your* genetics isn’t about control; it’s about feeling fully "yours" in a way that adoption (even with donor sperm) might not provide. That’s valid, even if it’s not your priority. - **The 25% risk isn’t "small."** For her, it’s a gut-wrenching gamble. For you, it’s a line you won’t cross. That’s okay—**but you can’t force her to see it that way.** Compassion isn’t about agreeing; it’s about acknowledging her pain. ### **3. You’re Both Stuck in a Deadlock** - **Her position:** "I want *your* biological child, even with risk." - **Your position:** "I won’t risk it, and adoption isn’t enough for me." This isn’t a debate to "win"—it’s a crisis where you’re both asking, *"How do we move forward together?"* Right now, you’re at an impasse because you’re both hurt, defensive, and unwilling to meet each other halfway. ### **4. What You *Can* Do (Even If You’re Pissed)** You said you don’t want to "extend the olive branch" first, but **this isn’t about who "caves" first—it’s about rebuilding trust.** Here’s how: - **Acknowledge her pain.** Even if you’re still angry, say something like: *"I know you’re hurting, and I don’t want to dismiss that. I love you, and I want us to figure this out together."* (This doesn’t mean you’re giving up your stance—just that you’re not shutting her out.) - **Give her space to grieve.** She’s not "dramatic" for being upset—she’s processing a devastating reality. Pushing her to "get over it" will only deepen the wound. - **Seek help.** Therapy (individual or couples) could help you both process this without blame. A neutral third party might help you see each other’s perspectives. - **Re-evaluate adoption.** If she’s open to it, could you explore it *after* trying IVF with PGT (preimplantation genetic testing) to reduce the risk? Some couples do this to balance her desire for biological connection with your comfort level. - **Check your own fears.** Are you avoiding adoption because it feels like "giving up" on your dream, or because you’re afraid of not being a "real" father? Adoption is just as valid as biological parenthood. ### **5. The Bigger Picture** You’re both young, and this isn’t the end of your family story. But right now, you’re in a **marriage crisis**—not just about kids, but about how you handle conflict, fear, and love. If you can’t navigate this with compassion, other issues will fester. ### **Final Thought:** You’re not an asshole for wanting to protect your child from blindness—but you *are* an asshole for hurting her in the process. **The goal isn’t to "win" this argument; it’s to find a way to love each other through it.** That might mean compromise, therapy, or even accepting that you may not have the same family as you imagined—but it *has* to start with you showing up for her, even when you’re angry. --- **TL;DR:** You’re not wrong for your stance, but you’re wrong for how you’re handling it. Right now, you need to **stop, listen, and try to meet her in the middle**—even if it’s just to say, *"I see how much this hurts you, and I’m here."* If you can’t do that, you’re both in trouble. But if you can, there’s still hope.
